target.title: High performance communication by people with paralysis using an intracortical brain-computer interface

read.pdf: Fig. 1a/b, Fig. 2a–g, Figs. 3–5, Fig. 1–4 supplements, Tables 1–3 (captions/rows rendered in text.txt); no PDF or visual figure files supplied.

entries.text: The evaluation enrolled three BrainGate2 clinical-trial participants: T6 and T7 with ALS and T5 with spinal-cord injury.
entries.condition: Human intracortical BCI study; participants had severe motor impairment; individual protocols differed.

entries.text: T6 was a 51-year-old woman with ALS who retained dexterous finger and wrist movements.
entries.condition: T6; ALS; female; right-handed; retained dexterous finger/wrist movement; one 96-channel array; results span post-implant days 570, 572, 577, 588, 591, 602, 605, and 621.

entries.text: T5 was a 63-year-old man with C4 ASIA C spinal cord injury and limited reproducible limb movement.
entries.condition: T5; right-handed; spinal-cord injury about 9 years before enrollment; two 96-channel arrays; only weak non-dominant elbow/finger movement was reproducible; data from post-implant days 56, 57, 68, and 70.

entries.text: T7 was a 54-year-old man with ALS and very limited, inconsistent finger movement.
entries.condition: T7; right-handed; two 96-channel arrays; data from post-implant days 539 and 548; died before planned HMM sessions, for reasons unrelated to the trial.

entries.text: Neural activity came from 96-channel intracortical silicon arrays in motor-cortex hand/upper-extremity areas.
entries.condition: T6 had one 1.0-mm array; T5 and T7 had two 1.5-mm arrays each. Arrays were implanted in dominant motor cortex; no noninvasive sensing modality was used.
entries.loc: Figure 1 caption | Materials and methods: Participants

entries.text: The NeuroPort sampled each channel at 30 kSamples/s after analog band-pass filtering from 0.3 Hz to 7.5 kHz.
entries.condition: All neural channels; real-time processing used Simulink/xPC. Common-average referencing was applied before spike and HF-LFP feature extraction.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural feature extraction

entries.text: Signals were common-average referenced; spikes were threshold crossings and HF-LFP features were band power from 150–450 Hz.
entries.condition: T6 continuous control used hybrid spike and HF-LFP features; T5 and T7 continuous control used spikes only. T6 HMM used HF-LFP; T5 HMM used spikes.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural feature extraction

entries.text: Spike-detection thresholds were array-specific: T6 −50 μV; T5 −95 μV; T7 lateral −70 μV and medial −90 μV.
entries.condition: Threshold detector applied every millisecond; threshold value differed by participant/array.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural feature extraction

entries.text: Calibration labels came from T6 finger movement, T5/T7 attempted movement during open-loop cursor trajectories, then closed-loop neural control.
entries.condition: T6 movement calibration mapped index finger/thumb to cursor axes; T5/T7 followed preprogrammed trajectories and attempted movements. T5 also attempted ipsilateral hand squeeze for selection. T6 movement-suppression/free-typing sessions used imagined movement in open-loop calibration.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms

entries.text: Each evaluation used session-collected calibration data; T6 recalibrated decoders by blockset, while T5/T7 retained decoders and updated velocity bias.
entries.condition: Initial calibration, closed-loop recalibration, then blockset-level calibration/bias update; once quantitative data collection began, the initial calibration stage could not be restarted.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms; Quantitative performance evaluations

entries.text: Continuous cursor control used the ReFIT Kalman Filter; click classification used a two-state HMM for T6/T5, but not T7.
entries.condition: ReFIT-KF: two-dimensional cursor movement. HMM state posteriors used PCA-reduced features and Gaussian state models; top 4 PCs were retained after empirical 3–4-PC tuning. T6 HMM used HF-LFP; T5 HMM used spikes.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms

entries.text: Neural features were binned every 15 ms; velocity was integrated at 1 ms and the display refreshed at 120 Hz.
entries.unit: ms bins; ms position integration; Hz display refresh
entries.condition: ReFIT-KF and HMM received 15-ms bins; newest cursor position was integrated/displayed at the faster rates stated. HMM click required two consecutive bins above threshold.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms

entries.text: The HMM click threshold was the 93rd percentile of retraining-block state estimates; T7 bias adaptation used τ=30 s.
entries.condition: Click generated after two consecutive 15-ms bins exceeded the unsupervised threshold. T7 bias estimate updated with 1-ms step when speed exceeded a threshold roughly at the 10–20th speed quantile.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms

entries.text: Feature choice used tuning-significance ranking and cross-validated directional-decoding accuracy; the smallest feature set maximizing accuracy was selected.
entries.condition: For ReFIT-KF, neural features were added in p-value rank order; offline cross-validation was used to estimate online directional control quality. HMM used all available features of its selected signal type, then PCA.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms

entries.text: T6/T5 used 1-s reset-on-exit dwell or HMM click; T7 used cumulative 1.5-s dwell and recentered after selection.
entries.unit: seconds dwell; seconds dwell; ms recenter lockout
entries.condition: T6/T5 dwell counter reset when cursor left a target; T7 cumulative dwell counter persisted across visits to that target. T7 cursor recentered after each selection and selection was disabled for 500 ms.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Target selection and cursor re-centering

entries.text: Table 2 reports prior BCI experience of 1.5 years for T6/T7 and 9 prior sessions (about 1 month) for T5.
entries.condition: Prior BCI experience at the time of this study; Table 2 also lists a three-participant study average of 1 year. The author response says T6/T7 performed 2–3 research sessions weekly over 1.5 years.

entries.text: Copy typing used prompted sentences in fixed 2-minute blocks; T6/T5 used QWERTY and OPTI-II, while minimally experienced T7 used ABCDEF and OPTI-II.
entries.condition: Five evaluation days/21 typing blocks per layout for T6; two days/14 per layout for T5; two days/5–6 blocks per layout for T7. Task order within each blockset was pseudo-randomized subject to the two copy-typing blocks being adjacent; the same prompted sentence was used across both keyboard layouts in each blockset.
entries.loc: Results | Materials and methods: Quantitative performance evaluations

entries.text: T6 free-paced, free-choice question-and-answer typing averaged 24.4 ± 3.3 correct characters/min over 96 minutes across 3 days.
entries.condition: T6 only; OPTI-II keyboard; spontaneous responses to prompts; 96 minutes over 3 days. She could enable/disable the keyboard and used HMM click or 1-s dwell; asked to suppress hand movements as best she could.

entries.text: T6 copy-typed at 23.9 ± 6.5 ccpm on QWERTY.
entries.condition: T6; QWERTY; two-minute prompted copy-typing blocks across 5 days; 21 evaluation blocks; quantitative protocol measured peak performance.

entries.text: T6 copy-typed at 31.6 ± 8.7 ccpm on OPTI-II.
entries.condition: T6; OPTI-II; two-minute prompted copy-typing blocks across 5 days; 21 evaluation blocks; no word completion/prediction.

entries.text: T5 copy-typed at 36.1 ± 0.9 ccpm on QWERTY.
entries.condition: T5; QWERTY; two-minute prompted copy-typing blocks across 2 days; 14 evaluation blocks; no word completion/prediction.

entries.text: T5 copy-typed at 39.2 ± 1.2 ccpm on OPTI-II.
entries.condition: T5; OPTI-II; two-minute prompted copy-typing blocks across 2 days; 14 evaluation blocks; no word completion/prediction.

entries.text: T7 copy-typed at 13.5 ± 1.9 ccpm on ABCDEF.
entries.condition: T7; alphabetical ABCDEF keyboard substituted for unfamiliar QWERTY; two-minute copy-typing blocks across 2 days; 5–6 blocks per layout; no HMM click decoder.

entries.text: T7 copy-typed at 12.3 ± 4.9 ccpm on OPTI-II.
entries.condition: T7; OPTI-II; two-minute copy-typing blocks across 2 days; 5–6 blocks per layout; dwell selection and cursor recentering; no HMM click decoder.

entries.text: Across the three personalized best-layout copy-typing results, the table reports a study mean of 28.1 ccpm and 2.4 bps.
entries.condition: Table 1 current-study average (N=3); typing value is participant-specific best-layout rate (T6 OPTI-II, T5 OPTI-II, T7 ABCDEF); bitrate is participant mean on 6×6 grid.

entries.text: The direct prior typing benchmark was 9.4 ccpm for participant S3 in Bacher et al. (2015), without word completion.
entries.condition: Single participant S3; intracortical BCI; closed-loop calibration plus LDA; brainstem stroke; cited as the previous highest BCI typing rate without word completion. The target paper gives no more task-level condition for this value.

entries.text: The authors report copy-typing improvements of 3.4× for T6/OPTI-II, 4.2× for T5/OPTI-II, and 1.4× for T7/ABCDEF over the prior 9.4-ccpm benchmark.
entries.condition: T6/T5 used OPTI-II and T7 used ABCDEF; comparator Bacher et al. 2015, 9.4 ccpm; paper says comparator did not include word completion.
entries.quote: These results represent a 3.4x (T6, OPTI-II), 4.2x (T5, OPTI-II), and 1.4x (T7, ABCDEF) increase

entries.text: Typing-rate comparisons against the prior 9.4-ccpm report were significant at p<0.01 for all three participants (single-sided Mann–Whitney U tests).
entries.condition: T6/OPTI-II, T5/OPTI-II, and T7/ABCDEF versus the Bacher et al. 2015 9.4-ccpm high; single-sided Mann–Whitney U tests.

entries.text: The information-throughput benchmark was a two-minute 6×6 grid with randomly cued targets; bitrate subtracts errors and counts timeouts in elapsed time.
entries.condition: N=36 targets (6×6); uniformly distributed random target prompts; achieved bitrate B=log2(N−1)×max(S−2E,0)/t; timeouts with no selection counted in elapsed time but not S/E. A separate 9×9 (N=81) condition was run only with T5.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Grid task; Achieved bitrate

entries.text: T6 averaged 2.2 ± 0.4 bps in 6×6-grid evaluations across 5 days and 21 blocks.
entries.condition: T6; standard 6×6 random-target grid; two-minute blocks; 5 evaluation days; 21 blocks; T6 used ReFIT-KF plus HMM click.

entries.text: T5 averaged 3.7 ± 0.4 bps in 6×6-grid evaluations across 4 days and 29 blocks.
entries.condition: T5; standard 6×6 random-target grid; two-minute blocks; Results text reports 4 evaluation days and 29 blocks (the Fig. 3b caption says 2 days); T5 used ReFIT-KF plus HMM click.

entries.text: T7 averaged 1.4 ± 0.1 bps in 6×6-grid evaluations across 2 days and 6 blocks.
entries.condition: T7; standard 6×6 random-target grid; two-minute blocks; 2 evaluation days; 6 blocks; continuous ReFIT-KF only, dwell selection, no HMM.

entries.text: The paper’s Table 1 reports a three-participant standard-grid bitrate average of 2.4 bps.
entries.condition: Current-study Table 1 average (N=3); participant-specific 6×6-grid results were T6 2.2, T5 3.7, and T7 1.4 bps.

entries.text: T5 averaged 4.16 ± 0.39 bps on a denser 9×9 grid over 2 days and 8 blocks; the authors call it their highest documented BCI communication rate for motor impairment.
entries.condition: T5 only; denser 9×9 grid (N=81); two evaluation days; 8 two-minute evaluation blocks; separate from the 6×6 results; Table 1 rounds this to 4.2 bps.

entries.text: T5’s 9×9-grid bitrate was significantly higher than its own 6×6-grid performance (p<0.01, Student’s t test).
entries.condition: T5; 9×9 dense grid versus standard 6×6 grid; separate evaluation blocks; Student’s t test.

entries.text: The cited prior achieved-bitrate results were 0.93 bps for T6 and 0.64 bps for T7 in Jarosiewicz et al. (2015).
entries.condition: T6 and T7; earlier intracortical study using RTI+LDA; paper notes the earlier report measured a free-typing task, unlike the current standard grid task.

entries.text: Relative to the previous bitrate highs, the authors report 2.4× for T6, 2.2× for T7, and 4.0× for T5.
entries.condition: T6/T7 compared with their Jarosiewicz et al. (2015) results; T5 compared with the highest participant in that earlier study; prior and current tasks differ, with the earlier study using free typing.
entries.quote: performance of the current methods represents a factor of 2.4 (T6) and 2.2 (T7) increase.

entries.text: Grid-bitrate comparisons with Jarosiewicz et al. were significant for T6 and T7 at p<0.01 (single-sided Mann–Whitney U tests).
entries.condition: T6 and T7 current bitrate versus their previous study results; single-sided Mann–Whitney U test; T5’s 4.0× comparison is not assigned this p-value in the text.

entries.text: The HMM selected the cued target correctly on 92.6% of T6’s 1,087 grid-task clicks.
entries.condition: T6; HMM-based click selection during grid evaluation; errors were primarily near the target edge according to the caption.
entries.quote: T6 clicked on the correct target 92.6% of the time (1007/1087 total clicks).

entries.text: The text reports 97.7% correct HMM clicks for T5 (2,325/2,379 clicks); the supplement caption’s panel lead-in inconsistently names T7.
entries.condition: Reported sentence identifies T5, consistent with the author response’s statement that T5 used HMM; preceding panel description in the supplement says T7, an internal label inconsistency.
entries.quote: T5 clicked on the correct target 97.7% of the time (2325/2379 total clicks).

entries.text: With movement suppression, T6’s calibration finger movement fell by median factors of 7.2 for index finger and 12.6 for thumb.
entries.condition: T6 dataglove measurements during movement-based versus imagined/open-loop calibration on trial days 570 versus 595; index finger and thumb analyzed separately; movement compared 600–1200 ms after target onset; paired Student’s t test p<0.01.

entries.text: T6 movement-suppressed performance differed by 0–20% from free-movement performance across grid, OPTI-II, and QWERTY tasks, with p>0.2 in each comparison.
entries.condition: T6; movement-suppression sessions on trial days 595 and 598; copy typing and grid; Student’s t tests; no statistically significant difference was reported.

entries.text: Movement-suppressed T6 averaged 28.6 ± 2.0 ccpm on OPTI-II and 19.9 ± 4.3 ccpm on QWERTY.
entries.condition: T6; movement-suppressed calibration/control sessions; copy typing with OPTI-II and QWERTY; no word completion/prediction; compare free-movement values t20 and t19.

entries.text: The authors could not record EMG; finger movement was measured with a dataglove, so sub-threshold or nascent muscle activity was not directly measured.
entries.condition: Movement-suppression evidence concerns measured finger position and instructed effort; it does not directly quantify arm EMG or prove absence of muscle commands.

entries.text: Typing results intentionally excluded word prediction and word completion to measure the underlying BCI/interface performance.
entries.condition: Applies to the study’s typing-rate claims; the authors expect word-completion/prediction aids could increase effective overall communication rate but did not test them.

entries.text: Copy-typing performance depends on phrase difficulty and participants’ keyboard familiarity; T5/T7 were less familiar with layouts than T6.
entries.condition: Authors distinguish application-specific copy typing from the phrase/layout-independent random-target grid task.

entries.text: The ccpm metric treats uncorrected spelling/typographical errors as correct characters; only deleted characters reduce the net score.
entries.condition: C=max(S−2D,0)/t; S selections, D delete-key selections, t elapsed minutes; a character was considered incorrect only if the participant deleted it.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Correct characters per minute

entries.text: The quantitative protocol measured repeatable peak performance rather than system stability; long-term stability without explicit recalibration remained future work.
entries.condition: Calibration/bias updates were performed before measurement sets; sessions were not designed to quantify sustained performance without recalibration.

entries.text: T7 did not use HMM selection because he died before the planned HMM research sessions; he used continuous cursor control plus dwell selection.
entries.condition: T7’s evaluation therefore does not replicate the T6/T5 HMM configuration; death was unrelated to trial participation.
entries.quote: Unfortunately, however, T7 passed away before the HMM sessions could be conducted.

entries.text: The authors claim that all three participants exceeded previous BCI communication rates reported for people with motor impairment.
entries.condition: Supported by copy typing and grid-task comparisons in Table 1; T7 used no HMM, and the dense-grid record applies only to T5.

entries.text: The authors describe T6’s spontaneous free typing as the highest typing rate then reported for a person with physical disability using a BCI.
entries.condition: Claim concerns realistic, free-paced, free-choice responding by T6; distinct from standardized copy typing and grid-task results.

entries.text: The authors call T5’s 9×9 result the highest documented BCI communication rate then reported for a person with motor impairment.
entries.condition: T5 only; dense 9×9 grid; 4.16 ± 0.39 bps; separate from the all-participant 6×6 grid comparison.

entries.text: An ALS-user survey found 59% satisfied at 10–14 ccpm and 72% satisfied at 15–19 ccpm.
entries.condition: Survey of people with ALS about desired communication-BCI typing speed; these are respondent satisfaction proportions, not performance results from the target study.

entries.text: The discussion contrasts the BCI rates with able-bodied mobile-phone typing at 12–19 wpm, touch typing at 40–60 wpm, and speech at 90–170 wpm.
entries.condition: Contextual benchmarks cited from smartphone/text-entry, touch-typing, and speech literature; unlike the target BCI conditions, these use different users, tasks, and interfaces.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge surgical risks including bleeding, infection, seizure, and headache when discussing implanted versus external systems.
entries.condition: General risk discussion; the paper does not claim that the measured performance outweighs those risks for every individual.

entries.text: This was a research BrainGate2 system; the paper describes self-calibrating, fully implanted wireless operation only as a possible future system.
entries.condition: Implanted clinical-trial interface with task-based recalibration/bias updates; no claim that this study’s system was wireless, fully implanted electronics, or fully self-calibrating.

entries.text: A programming error truncated T6’s accessible OPTI-II copy-typing workspace halfway through the bottom keyboard row.
entries.condition: T6 OPTI-II copy-typing task only; differs from the other tasks whose workspace extended beyond the keyboard.

entries.text: No random seed or repeated-seed robustness analysis is reported for random grid targets or pseudorandomized task order.
entries.condition: Relevant to randomized target prompts and task/block ordering; the methods describe randomization but do not provide seed values or replicate runs across seeds.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Blocksets; Grid task

entries.text: Cross-validation fold construction and any independent validation/selection partition are not specified; decoder calibration and evaluation occurred in the same research session.
entries.condition: The paper mentions cross-validated feature selection and same-session training data, but does not state fold count, split unit, or whether feature-selection data were fully separate from reported evaluation blocks.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms

entries.text: No separate feature standardization/normalization procedure is specified beyond common-average referencing, band filtering, thresholding, power features, and PCA.
entries.condition: Neural preprocessing is described, but an additional scaling/normalization rule for feature vectors is not given.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural feature extraction

entries.text: No chance-level comparison or null-distribution result is reported for the grid, click-accuracy, or typing outcomes.
entries.condition: Grid target prompts were random and uniform, but the paper reports achieved bitrate and observed accuracy without a chance baseline or permutation test.

entries.text: No held-out participant cohort or independent external test site is reported; performance evidence is from the three enrolled participants and their repeated blocks.
entries.condition: The study reports per-participant clinical-trial sessions; T6 and T7 also appeared in the cited Jarosiewicz comparison, so that comparison is not participant-independent.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Quantitative performance evaluations

entries.text: T6 and T7 had also participated in Jarosiewicz et al. (2015); T5 was newly implanted and reached higher-than-T6 performance within 9 prior BCI sessions.
entries.condition: Training-history comparison from the author response; the authors argue prior experience alone does not explain the improvement, but did not run a dedicated learning-curve experiment.
entries.quote: Further, we have now added data from a new, recently-implanted participant (T5; implanted in Aug 2016, first BCI session Sept 2016, and data collected in Oct 2016)

entries.text: The authors note substantial between-participant performance variation and do not attribute it to one cause; disease effects, latency, familiarity, and experience may contribute.
entries.condition: T6/T5 rates exceeded T7’s; no controlled participant-level causal analysis was reported.

entries.text: The code was not linked publicly; it was platform-specific xPC code that could be requested from the corresponding author.
entries.condition: No public GitHub/repository URL is supplied, so there are no repository README or training/evaluation scripts to inspect for code-only conditions.

entries.text: Discussion converts the best-layout copy-typing rates to 6.3 wpm for T6, 7.8 wpm for T5, and 2.7 wpm for T7.
entries.condition: T6 OPTI-II 31.6 ccpm; T5 OPTI-II 39.2 ccpm; T7 ABCDEF 13.5 ccpm; all are standardized copy-typing averages without word prediction/completion.

entries.text: The authors note the prior bitrate study used free typing; they estimate cognitive-load differences in their own T6 free-versus-copy comparison at about 30%, less than the between-study 2–4× gap.
entries.condition: Authors’ rationale for why task cognitive load alone is unlikely to explain the Jarosiewicz comparison; free typing and copy typing are not identical evaluation conditions.

entries.text: The authors conclude that intracortical BCIs are a promising approach to assistive communication for people with paralysis.
entries.condition: Authors’ concluding interpretation of the three-participant research study; not evidence of a deployed commercial system.

entries.text: During free typing, T6 formulated answers at her own pace and could engage/disengage the keyboard with a play/pause control.
entries.condition: T6’s free-paced Q&A sessions used spontaneous response composition rather than prompted copy typing; selecting the play button enabled keyboard input.

entries.text: The authors assert their decoder runs faster and more accurately than a recent Kalman-filter report (Shanechi et al., 2017).
entries.condition: Comparison is to Shanechi et al. (2017), a different system and task; the paper reports no head-to-head benchmark for this claim.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms

entries.text: The authors use T5’s spike-only performance exceeding T6’s hybrid spike/HF-LFP performance to argue that spikes alone can support high-performance control.
entries.condition: Between-participant comparison: T5 3.7 bps with spikes only (t31) versus T6 2.2 bps with spikes plus HF-LFP (t30); different participants, arrays, and days.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural feature extraction

entries.text: The authors argue eye-movement EMG is an unlikely driver of T6’s HF-LFP control, based on spiking similarity, an eyes-closed task, and T5’s spike-only result.
entries.condition: No EMG or eye tracking was recorded; the evidence is indirect (HF-LFP versus spike similarity, eyes-closed auditory-cued movements, and T5’s spike-only performance).
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural feature extraction

entries.text: T6 continued to move her hand during the quantitative evaluations, so residual movement is a potential confound for her high performance.
entries.condition: Authors address this with separate movement-suppressed sessions (trial days 595 and 598), but EMG was not recorded (t44) and free-moving closed-loop glove data are missing (t77).

entries.text: During free typing T6 was asked to suppress hand movements, whereas during quantitative evaluations she was free to move.
entries.condition: Different movement instructions across the spontaneous and standardized tasks, so free-typing performance is not directly comparable to free-movement copy-typing or grid results.
entries.loc: Video 1 caption | Materials and methods: Free typing task

entries.text: The authors did not run dedicated learning experiments, so training and BCI-experience effects were not measured.
entries.condition: They instead compare prior experience in Table 2 (t16) and cite a direct T6/T7 comparison with Jarosiewicz et al. (2015).

entries.text: The authors argue the improvement is unlikely to be explained by BCI experience because participants’ experience was comparable to prior studies.
entries.condition: Table 2 lists 1.5 years for T6/T7, 9 sessions (~1 month) for T5, and prior-study experience; no formal learning-curve test was run (t75).

entries.text: Finger positions during closed-loop control were not recorded in freely moving sessions, preventing a free-versus-suppressed closed-loop movement comparison.
entries.condition: Suppression was quantified during calibration for free versus suppressed sessions and during closed-loop only for suppressed sessions; EMG was absent.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Quantifying movement suppression

entries.text: A direct comparison with T6’s earlier eye-gaze speller was impossible because she had left the clinical trial.
entries.condition: The paper therefore compares against published BCI rates rather than the participant’s own AAC system (t62, t50).

entries.text: Internal inconsistency: the Results report T5 grid testing over 4 days and 29 blocks, while the Fig. 3b caption says 2 days.
entries.condition: Results text: “4 days of testing with T5 ( Figure 3b ; 29 grid evaluation blocks)”; the caption’s count conflicts with it. See t31 for the performance value.

entries.text: The paper’s summary claims all three participants achieved the highest BCI communication rates reported to date for people with movement impairment.
entries.condition: Based on copy typing and grid comparisons in Table 1; T7 used no HMM, and T5’s densest-grid record is a separate 9×9 condition (t32, t49, t34).

entries.text: The abstract frames the result as demonstrating the potential utility of iBCIs as powerful assistive communication devices.
entries.condition: Interpretive claim from a three-participant research study; not evidence of a deployed consumer or home-use system.

entries.text: T6 and T7 data were collected 1.5 years after array implantation, which the authors cite as evidence of multi-year intracortical usefulness.
entries.condition: T6 days 570–621 and T7 days 539/548; T5 was newly implanted (days 56–70), so the long-term claim rests on T6/T7.

entries.text: T5’s click decoder was trained on the same block as the cursor decoder; T6 used a separate HMM calibration and T7 had no HMM.
entries.condition: T6 had a dedicated HMM click calibration; T7’s sessions calibrated only the cursor decoder. T6 HMM used HF-LFP and T5 HMM used spikes (t11, t97).

entries.text: T6 typed free responses on the OPTI-II optimized keyboard layout, chosen to minimize cursor travel for English text.
entries.condition: OPTI-II from Rick (2010); also used for copy typing by T6/T5/T7; no word prediction or completion (t45, t94).

entries.text: Copy typing used seven sentences: a pangram, easy common phrases, the Rainbow Passage opening, and conversational sentences.
entries.condition: Sentence sources: pangram (Silfverberg et al., 2000), common phrases, Rainbow Passage (Fairbanks, 1960), and conversational sentences; the same sentence was used across layouts within a blockset.

entries.text: T7’s cursor recentering after every selection was unsupervised and independent of selection correctness; the authors say it did not compromise typing or bitrate measurement.
entries.condition: Recentering occurred after correct and incorrect selections, followed by a 500-ms selection lockout; T6/T5 did not recenter (t15).
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Target selection and cursor re-centering

entries.text: The HMM emitted a click only after click-state probability exceeded threshold for two consecutive 15-ms bins.
entries.condition: Threshold was the 93rd percentile of retraining-block state estimates (t13); T6/T5 could also use dwell selection.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms

entries.text: No held-out test-day condition is reported; every blockset followed same-session calibration or bias update.
entries.condition: Reported performance is therefore not a frozen-decoder generalization test across days; the paper supplies no independent test session or participant-held-out split.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms

entries.text: Calibration sample sizes for T5/T7 open-loop blocks and HMM retraining are not reported; only T6’s 112-trial glove calibration is specified.
entries.condition: T5/T7 used open-loop calibration instead; the text does not give their calibration trial counts or the HMM retraining sample sizes.

entries.text: No per-sentence typing results are reported, so phrase difficulty cannot be separated from layout or participant effects.
entries.condition: Sentences varied across blocksets; only aggregate participant/layout means and selected video examples are reported (t46).

entries.text: No multiple-comparison correction is reported across the typing, bitrate, click-accuracy, dense-grid, and movement-suppression tests.
entries.condition: The paper reports several p<0.01 and p>0.2 tests but does not state a family-wise or false-discovery correction.

entries.text: T5’s protocol was changed after T6/T7 to use bias updates, constant decoders, and same-block HMM training, so participant protocols were not identical.
entries.condition: The scientific protocol used with T5 reflected advances from the prior two participants; Table 3 summarizes differing decoders, dwell times, bias correction, recentering, and recalibration.
entries.loc: Materials and methods | Neural control algorithms

entries.text: Jarosiewicz et al. (2015) reported a four-participant average of 0.59 bps, with T6 0.93, T7 0.64, S3 0.58, and T2 0.19 bps.
entries.condition: RTI+LDA; ALS 2, brainstem stroke 2. The table marks average typing rate n/a because that study’s typing rates included word prediction/completion; the prior study used a free-typing task.

entries.text: The authors claim word completion or prediction would only increase effective typing rates.
entries.condition: No word-completion or prediction algorithm was tested; this is an expectation, not a measured result (t45).
entries.quote: Further additions of word completion or prediction should only increase the effective typing rates.

entries.text: Free-typing sessions were not optimized for filter calibration; performance was maintained by evaluation or recalibration blocks at the participant’s or researchers’ discretion.
entries.condition: Free typing is therefore less standardized than the quantitative copy-typing/grid protocol (t48).

entries.text: Grid timeouts are included in elapsed time but not in selections or errors; timeout counts are not reported.

questions.q: Which reported rate best represents spontaneous communication, and how does it differ from the peak standardized tests?
questions.answer: The closest spontaneous-use result is T6’s free-paced question-and-answer rate of 24.4 ± 3.3 ccpm over 96 minutes across three days (t18), which is below her standardized OPTI-II copy-typing mean of 31.6 ± 8.7 ccpm (t20); the authors attribute about 30% of that gap to cognitive load (t67). Free typing was not optimized for calibration and used discretion-based recalibration (t95).

questions.q: Was the improvement dependent on the HMM click decoder?
questions.answer: The main typing and bitrate results for T6/T5 used the HMM click decoder (t11, t83), but T7 reached 13.5 ccpm and 1.4 bps with dwell selection and no HMM (t23, t32, t49). The paper does not isolate the HMM’s contribution within a participant; T7’s no-HMM result is between-participant, and HMM click accuracy is benchmarked separately (t39, t40, t98).

questions.q: What are the key prior benchmarks, and are those comparisons fully like-for-like?
questions.answer: The direct typing baseline is Bacher et al.’s 9.4 ccpm (t26), against which the paper reports 1.4×–4.2× gains (t27, t28), and the prior bitrate baseline is Jarosiewicz et al.’s 0.93/0.64 bps for T6/T7 (t36, t93), against which it reports 2.4×/2.2× and 4.0× for T5 (t37, t38). The prior study used free typing, the current comparisons differ in task and some prior studies include word prediction (t45, t67, t93, t102).

questions.q: What decoding, sensing, and language-model conditions should a reviewer preserve?
questions.answer: The system used 96-channel intracortical arrays (t5), 30-kS/s sampling with CAR and spike/HF-LFP features (t6, t7, t60), array-specific thresholds (t8), ReFIT-KF plus a two-state HMM for T6/T5 (t11), 15-ms bins (t12), a 93rd-percentile click threshold over two bins (t13, t87), 1/1.5-s dwell rules (t15), and no word prediction or completion (t45, t94). T6 used hybrid features while T5/T7 used spikes only (t97).

questions.q: What validity and generalization caveats should be foregrounded?
questions.answer: The ccpm metric counts uncorrected spelling errors as correct (t47), copy typing depends on phrase difficulty and keyboard familiarity (t46), calibration and evaluation occurred in the same session without a held-out test day (t88, t59), calibration sample sizes for T5/T7 are absent (t89), no seeds or chance baseline are reported (t58, t61), and the three participants used different protocols (t92, t107). Movement suppression was addressed but EMG was not recorded and free-movement closed-loop glove data are missing (t44, t73, t77).

questions.q: Are public code details available to verify omitted training or evaluation conditions?
questions.answer: No public repository is linked. The paper says its xPC code may be made available on request (t65), so no repository-only condition such as a code-level seed, split, or normalization rule can be recovered.

questions.q: Which confounds could explain the performance gains, and how did the authors control them?
questions.answer: BCI experience was compared but not experimentally controlled (t16, t63, t75, t76); T6’s residual movement was addressed with suppression sessions but EMG was not recorded and free-movement closed-loop glove data are missing (t41, t42, t43, t73, t77); task cognitive load and protocol changes also differ (t67, t92, t107).

questions.q: Which results are internally inconsistent or most fragile?
questions.answer: T5’s grid duration is 4 days/29 blocks in the Results but 2 days in the Fig. 3b caption (t31, t79), and the HMM supplement’s panel lead-in names T7 while reporting T5’s 97.7% accuracy (t40). T7 had no HMM, and the pooled three-participant averages mix different configurations (t49, t50, t80, t108).

questions.q: What evidence supports that HF-LFP rather than eye-muscle artifact drove T6’s performance?
questions.answer: Only indirect evidence: HF-LFP resembled spiking, an eyes-closed auditory-cued task showed similar modulation, and T5 achieved higher performance with spikes alone; no EMG or eye tracking was recorded (t71, t72, t44).

questions.q: Does the target report any within-participant comparison of HMM click versus dwell-only selection, or the share of selections made by click versus dwell?
questions.answer: No. Every 'dwell' passage (Methods: Target selection; Table 3; Videos 1 and 6; Discussion; decision letter) describes the rules only; T6/T5 could use either method in the same block and no split is reported.

questions.q: Are Kim et al. 2011, Bacher et al. 2015 and Kao et al. 2016 in the wiki?
questions.answer: No (index search by title); their designs are taken from the target's Table 1 and Fig. 3-figure supplement 1 only.
